blocks.heading: Creating Your FastAPI Application
blocks.body: To start building your API, you first import the `FastAPI` class from the `fastapi` package. Then, you create an instance of this class by calling it with parentheses and assign that new object to a variable named `app`. This `app` variable is the main point of interaction for creating all your API routes.

blocks.heading: Defining a Path Operation Decorator
blocks.body: To handle requests, use the `@app.get` decorator above your function. The first argument is the path (e.g., "/"). This tells FastAPI which URL and HTTP method to match.

items.title: Decorator Syntax
items.text: Place `@app.get("/path")` immediately above your function definition.

items.title: Path Specification
items.text: The path string goes inside the parentheses, like "/" for the root.

blocks.title: Root GET Route Example

blocks.heading: Path Parameter Types and Conversion

blocks.heading: Mixing Path Parameters and Request Bodies

items.title: Request Body Declaration

items.title: Automatic Distinction

m4-s1.title: Declare a Pydantic model with mixed Path, Query, and Body parameters using `Field` for validation.
m4-s1.summary: Use Pydantic Field to add validation and metadata to model attributes while mixing Path, Query, and Body parameters.
you_will_learn: Import Field from pydantic
Add constraints like max_length or gt
Mix Path, Query, and Body in one endpoint

blocks.heading: Using Field with Mixed Parameters
blocks.body: Import `Field` from `pydantic` to add metadata or validation rules to Pydantic model attributes. You can mix `Path`, `Query`, and `Body` parameters in a single endpoint function signature. FastAPI automatically recognizes the source based on parameter type and location.

items.title: Import Field Correctly
items.text: Import `Field` from `pydantic`, not `fastapi`. It works like `Query` or `Body` but for model attributes.

items.title: Add Validation Rules
items.text: Use `Field(gt=0, max_length=300)` to set constraints directly on model fields like price or description.

items.title: Mix Parameter Types
items.text: Combine path, query, and body parameters in one function; FastAPI handles each source automatically.

blocks.title: Mixed Parameters with Field Validation
blocks.code:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, Path
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = Field(default=None, max_length=300)
    price: float = Field(gt=0, description="Price must be positive")

@app.put("/items/{item_id}")
async def update_item(
    item_id: Annotated[int, Path(title="Item ID", ge=0)],
    q: str | None = None,
    item: Item | None = None,
):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q, "item": item}

blocks.text: Remember that `Field` is imported from `pydantic`, while `Path`, `Query`, and `Body` come from `fastapi`.

m4-s2.title: Define nested models where attributes are lists or sets of submodels with type parameters.

blocks.heading: Declaring List and Set Attributes
blocks.body: To define an attribute as a list or set, use standard Python type syntax with square brackets. For a list of strings, write `list[str]`. For a set of unique strings, write `set[str]`. You can also nest Pydantic models inside these types, such as `list[Image]`, to accept a JSON array of objects.

items.title: List Type Syntax
items.text: Use `list[T]` where T is the element type, for example `list[str]` or `list[Image]`.

items.title: Set Type Syntax
items.text: Use `set[T]` to enforce unique items, such as `set[str]` for a set of strings.

items.title: Nested Model Lists
items.text: Combine list and model types like `list[Image]` to accept an array of submodel objects.

blocks.title: Model with List and Set Attributes
blocks.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Image(BaseModel):
    url: str
    name: str

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    tags: set[str] = set()
    images: list[Image] | None = None

blocks.text: FastAPI automatically converts JSON arrays into the declared list or set type, handling duplicates for sets.

items.title: Annotate with response_model
items.text: Pass the output model to the `response_model` parameter of the path operation decorator to enable filtering.

items.title: Automatic Filtering
items.text: FastAPI filters the returned data to match only the fields declared in the output response model.

blocks.title: Filter Password from Response
blocks.code:
from typing import Any

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr

app = FastAPI()


class UserIn(BaseModel):
    username: str
    password: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None


class UserOut(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: EmailStr
    full_name: str | None = None


@app.post("/user/", response_model=UserOut)
async def create_user(user: UserIn) -> Any:
    return user

blocks.text: If you use `response_model_exclude_unset=True`, only explicitly set fields appear in the JSON response, omitting defaults.

m4-s4.title: Configure a response to return a Union of multiple types or an arbitrary dict with typed keys and values.
m4-s4.summary: Learn to return Union types or typed arbitrary dicts in FastAPI responses.
you_will_learn: Use typing.Union for multiple response types
Place specific types before general ones
Declare dict[str, float] for key-value pairs
Apply response_model to the decorator

blocks.heading: Flexible Response Types with Union and Dict
blocks.body: To return a `Union` of models, use `typing.Union` (or Python 3.10+ union syntax) in the `response_model`. Order matters: put the most specific type first (e.g., `PlaneItem`) before less specific ones (e.g., `CarItem`). For arbitrary dicts, declare keys and values explicitly like `dict[str, float]`. FastAPI validates and serializes data based on these types.

items.title: Union Order Matters
items.text: Always list the most specific type first in a Union to ensure correct validation logic.

items.title: Typed Dict Responses
items.text: Use `dict[key_type, value_type]` to define responses with specific key and value types.

items.title: Decorator Parameter
items.text: Set the `response_model` argument on the route decorator, not inside the function signature.

blocks.title: Union Response Example

blocks.text: Remember that JSON keys are always strings. FastAPI converts string keys to integers if they contain pure numeric values.

m5-s1.title: Raise an HTTPException with a specific status code and custom headers to return a structured error response.
m5-s1.summary: Learn to raise HTTPException with custom status codes and headers for structured error responses.
you_will_learn: Import HTTPException from FastAPI
Pass status_code argument when raising
Add custom headers to errors
Return structured JSON error details

blocks.heading: Raising Custom HTTP Errors with Headers
blocks.body: To return a specific error response, import `HTTPException` from FastAPI. When an error occurs in your endpoint logic, raise the exception instead of returning normally. You can pass `status_code` to set the HTTP status (e.g., 404) and `detail` for a JSON message. For advanced scenarios like security headers, you can also pass a dictionary of custom headers.

items.title: Importing the Exception
items.text: Use `from fastapi import HTTPException` to access the exception class in your code.

items.title: Setting Status and Detail
items.text: Pass `status_code` as an integer (like 404) and `detail` as a string or dict for the error body.

items.title: Adding Custom Headers
items.text: Include a `headers` dictionary argument to attach custom metadata to the error response.

blocks.title: Raising an Error with Headers

blocks.text: Remember to `raise` the exception, do not `return` it. The code inside your endpoint stops executing immediately when raised.

m5-s2.title: Define a dependency function that accepts query parameters and returns a dictionary of values.
m5-s2.summary: Learn to define reusable dependency functions with query parameters using Depends() and Annotated.
you_will_learn: Declare a function returning a dict as a dependency
Use Annotated to combine type hints with Depends
Share the dependency annotation across multiple endpoints

blocks.heading: Define Reusable Dependencies with Query Parameters
blocks.body: Create an async function that accepts query parameters and returns a dictionary. Use `Depends()` in your endpoint parameter to tell FastAPI to call this function automatically. Wrap the return type and `Depends()` inside `Annotated` to preserve type information for your editor.

items.title: Declare the Dependency Function
items.text: Define an async function that accepts query parameters like `q`, `skip`, and `limit`, then return a dictionary containing those values.

items.title: Use Annotated with Depends
items.text: Combine the return type hint (e.g., `dict`) and `Depends(dependency_function)` inside `Annotated` to let FastAPI handle injection correctly.

items.title: Share the Annotation
items.text: Store the `Annotated[...]` value in a variable to reuse it across multiple endpoints without repeating the full definition.

blocks.title: Reusable Dependency with Query Parameters
blocks.code:
from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

async def common_parameters(q: str | None = None, skip: int = 0, limit: int = 100):
    return {"q": q, "skip": skip, "limit": limit}

CommonsDep = Annotated[dict, Depends(common_parameters)]

@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

@app.get("/users/")
async def read_users(commons: CommonsDep):
    return commons

blocks.text: FastAPI calls your dependency function automatically when a request arrives. Do not call it manually in your endpoint code.

docs.label: Use `Annotated` in the type for the `q` parameter

m5-s3.title: Create a class that acts as a dependency by implementing __init__ and using it with Depends().
m5-s3.summary: Learn how to use Python classes as FastAPI dependencies with Annotated and Depends.
you_will_learn: Define a class with __init__ parameters
Use Annotated to declare the dependency type
Pass the class directly to Depends()
Access dependency attributes in endpoints

blocks.heading: Classes as Dependencies
blocks.body: A Python class is callable, so FastAPI treats it like a function. Define your class with an __init__ method containing parameters. Use Annotated to wrap the class type in your endpoint parameter and pass the class itself (not an instance) to Depends(). This allows FastAPI to extract arguments for validation.

items.title: Define the Class
items.text: Create a class with __init__ parameters that match the data you need in your endpoint.

items.title: Use Annotated
items.text: Wrap the class type in Annotated to tell FastAPI how to handle it as a dependency.

items.title: Pass the Class
items.text: Pass the class itself to Depends(), not an instance, so FastAPI can instantiate it.
